title: The Opera Game
subtitle: Paul Morphy vs Duke Karl / Count Isouard — Paris, 1858

intro.text: Paris, eighteen fifty-eight. Paul Morphy is at the opera, half-watching the music, while two noblemen share the Black pieces against him. What follows is the most famous miniature ever played. Watch how Morphy turns every piece toward the enemy king — and how a couple of quiet Black slips open the floodgates.

segments.text: Black settles for the solid but passive Philidor.
The bishop pins the knight — but it'll soon become a target.
Bishop to c4, eyeing the soft f7 square.

Black develops naturally, but this is the first real mistake. Nf6 blocks the queen from defending b7 — Stockfish wanted Qf6 instead, where the queen covers b7 and f7 from one square. Now Morphy's pieces pour toward the queenside with a free hand.
Qb3 — hitting b7 and f7 at once.
Qe7 is the only way to defend both.
Morphy ignores the loose pawn and just keeps developing.
c6 shores up the light squares, but the king is stuck in the centre.
The last piece arrives, pinning the f6 knight.
Desperate for air, Black plays b5 — an inaccuracy that loosens everything. The engine preferred the quiet Na6. Instead, b5 throws open exactly the lines Morphy has been aiming at.
And Morphy strikes — the knight crashes into b5. It's a sacrifice, but after the recapture the checks and pins come so fast that Black's pieces never get a chance to breathe.
Forced — the knight has to be taken.
Bxb5, check, and the bishop rejoins with tempo.
Blocking with the knight, which is now pinned and overloaded.
Castling long — the rook drops onto d1, straight at the pin.
Black adds a defender to the pin, but it won't be enough.
The exchange sacrifice — ripping away the defender.
Forced; anything else collapses at once.
The second rook piles onto the pin. Black is paralysed.
Qe6 — the only move that survives another beat.
Bxd7, check, removing the last defender.
Forced recapture — and now everything is set.
Here is the famous blow: Qb8+, a queen sacrifice, and the only move that wins. The knight must capture, because it's the one piece that can block the check — and that is exactly the point.
The knight takes the queen, stepping off d7.

Rook to d8 — checkmate. Morphy finishes with a single rook on the open file while Black's queen, bishop and knight all sit uselessly at home. That's the whole lesson: it isn't how many pieces you own, it's how many are actually fighting.

outro.text: Seventeen moves. Morphy developed every piece toward the king while Black shuffled on the defensive — and rapid development on open lines beat a material count every time. That's the Opera Game.
